"Implement the solution in src/lib.rs so that the tests in tests/forth.rs, tests/alloc-attack.rs pass. The specification follows.

# Instructions

Implement an evaluator for a very simple subset of Forth.

[Forth][forth]
is a stack-based programming language.
Implement a very basic evaluator for a small subset of Forth.

Your evaluator has to support the following words:

- `+`, `-`, `*`, `/` (integer arithmetic)
- `DUP`, `DROP`, `SWAP`, `OVER` (stack manipulation)

Your evaluator also has to support defining new words using the customary syntax: `: word-name definition ;`.

To keep things simple the only data type you need to support is signed integers of at least 16 bits size.

You should use the following rules for the syntax: a number is a sequence of one or more (ASCII) digits, a word is a sequence of one or more letters, digits, symbols or punctuation that is not a number.
(Forth probably uses slightly different rules, but this is close enough.)

Words are case-insensitive.

[forth]: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forth_%28programming_language%29


# Instructions append

Note the additional test case in `tests/alloc-attack.rs`. It tests against
algorithmically inefficient implementations. Because of that, it usually times
out online instead of outright failing, leading to a less helpful error message.


Do NOT modify the tests or the build files except as stated below. Do not create new files unless the specification requires them; Helper modules may go under src/; you may add [dependencies] from the offline crates listed in OFFLINE_CRATES.md to Cargo.toml."

## Implementation (`src/lib.rs`)

The evaluator keeps a value stack plus a **definition dictionary** (`Vec<Definition>` with a `HashMap<String, usize>` name index). The key design decision is how user-defined words are stored, which has to satisfy two tests that pull in opposite directions:

- **`can_use_different_words_with_the_same_name`** requires a definition to capture the meaning of words *at definition time* (`bar` keeps calling the old `foo`).
- **`alloc_attack`** forbids eagerly expanding sub-definitions into parent bodies (that would make `z`'s body 2²²⁶ tokens long).

The solution is the classic Forth "code address" approach: when parsing `: name body ;`, each word token in the body is resolved to an **index** into the dictionary (`Instr::Word(usize)`) rather than being inlined. Redefining a word appends a *new* dictionary entry and repoints the name map; old indices stay valid, so previously defined words keep referencing the old entry. Bodies are stored exactly as written — no expansion — so the attack definitions cost only a couple of instructions each.

Other details:

- **Built-ins** (`+ - * / dup drop swap over`) are just the first eight dictionary entries, so user definitions can override them (`: + * ;` works).
- **Parsing**: tokens are whitespace-separated; a number is an optional `-` followed by all-ASCII digits (a bare `-` is the subtraction word). Everything else is a case-insensitive word.
- **Errors**: stack underflow is checked on every pop; division by zero returns `DivisionByZero`; defining a name that parses as a number (`: 1 2 ;`) returns `InvalidWord`; unknown words return `UnknownWord`.
- **Execution** is a recursive interpreter over instruction indices; each instruction is copied out before recursing so no dictionary borrow is held across calls (this also sidesteps a borrow-checker conflict with the recursive `execute_def`).

No test files, build files, or dependencies were modified.
